FAIR WORKWEEK SCHEDULE CHECKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What did that schedule change just cost you?

Paste the posted schedule and every change made afterwards with the time the worker was told. The page finds shifts posted too late, shifts added, moved or cut inside the notice window with the premium pay each one triggers, and closing-then-opening shifts that break the rest rule. Export the result as a CSV for payroll.

A fair workweek or predictive scheduling check for restaurant, retail and hospitality managers. New to the rules? Read what predictive scheduling pay is, with a worked example.

1. Rules

The numbers behind the preset (edit any of them)

Presets are a starting point, not a legal reading. Cities amend these rules and apply them by employer size and industry. Check each number against your city's official guidance.

2. Posted schedule

3. Changes after posting

Paste a schedule and a posting time, then click Check.

Result

EmployeeShift startsIssueNotice (h)PremiumDetail

How it works

Late posting: a shift that starts less than the required number of days after the posting time is flagged. No dollar figure is added because the remedy differs by city.

Changes: adding hours or moving a shift without losing hours is measured against the add/move window, and cancelling or cutting a shift against the cut/cancel window. Notice is the time from when the worker was told to the earlier of the old and new start. The premium is the flat dollars plus the hours of pay, or the share of pay for the hours lost, from the boxes above.

Rest: after all changes are applied, any two shifts for the same person closer together than the minimum rest are flagged, and the hours that fall inside the rest window are priced at the multiplier. The worker's written consent is required to schedule it at all.

Not modelled: employer-size and industry coverage, emergency exceptions, daylight-saving shifts, and any city rule other than the numbers you can see. Worker-requested changes can be marked requested to exclude them.

Related tools: the shift roster builder to build the schedule in the first place, and the overtime pay calculator for the hours that spill past 40.

Checked: the test suite recomputes hand-worked Seattle and Chicago cases, including the exact boundary at 14 days and 24 hours.

Common questions

What is a fair workweek or predictive scheduling law?

A city or state rule that makes larger retail, restaurant and hospitality employers post work schedules in advance, usually 14 days, and pay the worker extra when the employer then adds hours, moves a shift or cancels one at short notice. Seattle, Chicago, New York City, Philadelphia, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Oregon each have their own version with different thresholds and different premiums.

How do I check a schedule for predictive scheduling violations?

Paste the posted schedule and the date it was posted, paste each later change with the time the worker was told, pick the city preset or type your own numbers, and the page lists every shift that was posted too late, every change made inside the notice window with the premium pay it triggers, and every closing-then-opening pair that breaks the rest rule.

How is predictability pay calculated?

It depends on the city. Under the Seattle and Chicago presets a change that adds hours or moves a shift inside 14 days costs one hour of pay at the worker's regular rate, and a cancellation or cut inside the window costs half the pay for the hours not worked. The page applies the numbers in the boxes, which you can overwrite to match the current text of your own ordinance.

Are these city numbers current and complete?

No promise. The presets are a starting point written from the public ordinance summaries, ordinances are amended, thresholds depend on employer size and industry, and there are exceptions such as worker-requested swaps and emergencies. Check the figures against your city's official page or your attorney before you rely on them, and edit any box that is out of date.

Does it handle worker-requested changes and emergencies?

Mark a change line with a final field of requested and the page counts no premium for it and reminds you to keep the written request. Emergency and other statutory exceptions are not modelled; leave those lines out and keep your own record.

Is my staff schedule uploaded anywhere?

No. Everything is calculated in your browser, nothing is sent to a server, and there are no accounts. Names stay on your device.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal advice and does not replace your city's ordinance, your payroll provider or an employment attorney. You are responsible for verifying every figure and every rule before you pay, withhold or document anything. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use. The presets summarise public ordinances and may be wrong, incomplete or out of date.

Independent. Not affiliated with any city, labour agency, payroll or scheduling software company, and none is named or ranked here. The example employees are invented.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record: nothing you enter is saved anywhere.

Everything runs in your browser. Your schedules and names are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded, csv_downloaded, text_shared) are counted only in local storage on your device, never with any of your data, and are switched off by Do Not Track.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

What is predictive scheduling pay? A worked example

Predictive scheduling laws, also called fair workweek laws, make covered restaurant, retail and hospitality employers do three things: post schedules ahead of time, pay extra when they change a posted shift at short notice, and leave a minimum rest between a closing shift and the next opening. The extra pay is easy to miss because it never appears as a line on the schedule. It appears as a change.

Open the free checker

The three triggers

Late posting. A schedule must go up a set number of days before the shift, 14 under the Seattle and Chicago presets. A shift that starts sooner than that after posting is flagged.

Short-notice change. Under the Seattle and Chicago presets, adding hours or moving a shift without cutting hours inside 14 days costs one hour of pay at the worker's regular rate. Cutting or cancelling a shift costs half the pay for the hours not worked: Seattle applies that inside 14 days, Chicago only inside 24 hours.

Rest. Ten hours between shifts. Scheduling less needs the worker's written consent and 1.25 times pay for the hours inside the window.

Worked example (Seattle preset)

The schedule is posted at 2026-10-05 09:00. Five shifts follow; four changes are made later. Rates are in the checker's example.

EmployeeWhat happenedNoticePremium
Ana ReyesShift cancelled (8 h at $20)24 h$80.00
Ben OkoyeFour-hour shift added48 h$15.00
Dee ParkShift cut from 8 h to 4 h (at $16)3 h$32.00
Dee ParkExtra shift added at her request—$0.00
Cy DahlCloses at 23:00, opens at 06:00: 7 h rest, 3 h inside the window (at $14)—$10.50

Total to review: $137.50. The same schedule under the Chicago preset costs less on the cancellation, because a cancel is only penalised inside 24 hours there.
